narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 51.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is just over 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, and both pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the second decile after your first year and the bottom decile after your third year, well below the average of accepted students who typically rank around the sixth decile. These low academic standings in law school were the main reasons the model doubted your likelihood of passing the bar.

Your LSAT score and undergraduate GPA worked in the opposite direction. Both were slightly above the averages of students who were accepted, and each modestly increased the model’s confidence that you would pass. However, these positive signals were not strong enough to overcome the negative impact of your class rankings.

The model did not consider your gender, race, or family income in reaching this outcome.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record and bar-exam readiness. Consider retaking key courses, seeking academic support, or gaining additional legal experience before reapplying. Improving your class standing or earning a higher LSAT score could meaningfully change future predictions in your favor.
